pages.text: A plain Create $(thing)Steam Engine$(0) bolted to a boiler still works as it always has: water and heat in, rotation out.$(br2)The $(thing)steam cycle$(0) is the advanced route. The boiler raises steam for a $(thing)Steam Turbine$(0) instead, and the steam that leaves the turbine is vented or condensed back into water. It takes more building, and in return it concentrates a lot of power in one place.

$(bold)The cycle at a glance$(0)$(br)$(li)A heated boiler turns water into $(thing)Pressurized Steam$(0).$(li)The turbine expands it into rotation.$(li)What leaves the turbine is $(thing)Low-Pressure Steam$(0).$(li)Vent it up a smokestack, or condense it back into water and send it to the boiler again.$(br2)No water is created or lost along the way: a full loop returns every drop.

pages.title: Steam Outlets
pages.text: Attach a Steam Engine to the boiler as usual, but put a $(thing)fluid pipe$(0) where its shaft would go. The engine no longer turns: it becomes an outlet that pipes out its share of the boiler as Pressurized Steam.

Each outlet takes the same share of the boiler that an engine would, so the boiler's size and heat level set how much steam you get: $(thing)10 mB per tick per boiler level$(0), the same water the boiler boils.$(br2)Engines and outlets can share one boiler, splitting its output between rotation and steam.

pages.title: The Steam Turbine
pages.text: A 7x7 multiblock of $(thing)Turbine Casing$(0) around a column of $(thing)Turbine Rotors$(0) fitted with blades. Pipe Pressurized Steam into the casing walls and take rotation from the cap rotor. It can stand up or lie on its side.

Every rotor layer adds speed and capacity, and burns about $(thing)8 mB of steam per tick$(0). A tall turbine needs a large boiler, or several.$(br2)$(li)$(thing)Stainless Steel Blades$(0): the first blades you can make. They waste part of the steam.$(li)$(thing)Titanium Blades$(0): full efficiency.$(br2)Engineer's Goggles on a rotor show height, blades, steam supply and exhaust.

$(bold)Exhaust$(0)$(br)Spent steam collects inside the turbine as Low-Pressure Steam. Pipe it out of any casing face.$(br2)If the exhaust tank fills up, the turbine shuts down and stops drawing steam until it is drained. A turbine with nowhere to send its exhaust will stall.

pages.title: Venting
pages.text: The simple answer: pipe the exhaust into a TFMG $(thing)Smokestack$(0) (brick, concrete or metal) or an $(thing)Exhaust$(0). It lets the steam out as white clouds. Cheap and reliable, but the water is lost, so the boiler needs a steady supply.

pages.title: Condensing
pages.text: To recover the water, pipe the exhaust into a $(thing)steel chemical vat$(0) of at least $(thing)4 tanks$(0) with a $(thing)Freezer$(0) at the bottom. It turns 1000 mB of steam into 1000 mB of water every second.

Each condensing vat handles about $(thing)50 mB per tick$(0), so a large boiler needs several in parallel.$(br2)The Freezer runs on electricity: feed it through a $(l:tfc:materialism_electricity/converter)Converter$(0) in output mode. Pipe the water back to the boiler and the loop is closed.

$(bold)Other steam sources$(0)$(br)The turbine burns Pressurized Steam from any source. A boiler is the usual one, but a $(thing)Solar Power Tower$(0) in steam mode and the $(thing)Fusion Reactor$(0) make it too. Their exhaust is handled the same way.
